newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Russia rejects NATO expansion plans at OSCE summit.
newsitem.headline: Russia rejects NATO expansion plans at OSCE summit.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, spoiling the party at a European security summit, told leaders from more than 50 nations on Monday that Moscow rejected NATO's plans to expand eastwards.

His tough line was backed by Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko. But it put Moscow at odds with most other European nations and threatened to sour the atmosphere at the meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
"Yes, Russia has no veto on the alliance's expansion. But nobody has a veto on our right to defend our national interests," Chernomyrdin said at the start of the two-day Lisbon summit.
The 58-year-old prime minister was speaking on behalf of President Boris Yeltsin, who was unable to attend because he is still recovering after heart surgery on November 5.
"We have declared clearly, and declare clearly now, our firm opposition to the North Atlantic alliance's plans to move itself and its military infrastructure towards our territory," he said.
"Is it not clear that the appearance of new dividing lines would lead to a worsening of the whole geopolitical situation in the world?"
He set out a vision of the OSCE as a forum with a larger security role in the next century which would create a Europe without any divisions and keep all countries on an even footing.

But Russia has little support for its proposals for turning the OSCE into an organisation serving as a counterbalance to NATO. Chernomyrdin urged other countries to rethink their views on NATO enlargement.

"We are convinced that there is still time and that it makes sense to think -- what can NATO expansion lead to? If our common goal is a united and peaceful Europe, then can we achieve it through the enlargement of military alliances?" he said.
Russia says NATO's plans to take in countries of eastern and central Europe, which were once Moscow's allies in the now defunct Warsaw Pact, would threaten its security.

But NATO has made clear it will not go back on its plans, and a row over expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation could overshadow the OSCE meeting, just as it did the organisation's last summit in Budapest in 1994.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore tried to ease Moscow's fears, saying NATO was a defensive alliance.
Only Belarus, which will have NATO on its doorstep if Poland gains entry as expected, joined its ally Russia in opposing the Western alliance's expansion.
"Everything should be done to avoid steps which could cause a new division in Europe and sow the seeds of mutual mistrust and suspicion," Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko said.
Although NATO expansion looks inevitable, Russian officials have taken a tough line against it to try to satisfy an influential nationalist audience at home.
Moscow also hoped its pressure would encourage Western leaders to make concessions or be more understanding on other issues at the summit, especially at talks on arms control.
Negotiators agreed just before the start of the summit to a new round of talks on reducing conventional arms across Europe.
This was a gesture to Russian demands for a quick agreement on revising a treaty which limits the numbers of such weapons and where they can be placed.
